chunks: And from him from Fadala from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and Hammam from Shu'ayb from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and Uthman ibn Isa from Sama'ah and Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammam from al-Halabi, all of them from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): In

the mukatab (slave who has contracted manumission for a specified sum), when half of the sum is paid and he is partially freed, is his testimony accepted in divorce? He (Abu Abdillah) said: 'If with him there is a man and a woman.' And Abu Basir said: 'Otherwise, it is not accepted.' The way to reconcile these narrations is one of two things: either we attribute them to a form of taqiyya (dissimulation) because they agree with the schools of those who preceded Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) as we have clarified, or the other way is to attribute them to the fact that the testimony of slaves is not accepted for their masters, but is accepted for others, due to the place of suspicion arising from their being drawn to their masters. As for what was included in the narration of al-Halabi, Sama'ah, and Abu Basir that the testimony of the mukatab is accepted in divorce if a man and a woman testify with him, this confirms what we mentioned earlier regarding the permissibility of accepting the testimony of the slave, because the inclusion of the woman in testimony regarding divorce is only for a form of taqiyya, because we will clarify later, if God wills, that the testimony of women is not accepted in divorce. And that which reveals what we mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has contracted with his master to pay a specific sum for his freedom

ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of a partially freed slave (mukatab) accepted in Islamic divorce proceedings?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction in the narrations by offering two primary scholarly interpretations: either the acceptance of the mukatab's testimony is based on *taqiyya* (dissimulation) to align with earlier juristic schools, or it reflects the specific legal principle that slaves' testimony is accepted for non-masters to avoid bias. This analysis highlights the nuanced Shia approach to evidentiary rules, particularly the inclusion of women in divorce testimony as a pragmatic exception rather than a general rule.
